summary: Sixth-order light on a granite pier at the point of a shoal in the Providence River, lit 1872; the 1938 hurricane left its dwelling unusable.

structures.note: Square tower built from the roof of the dwelling; 35 feet (11 m) from base to lantern.
Granite pier on which the 1872 beacon was set and which was enlarged in 1875.

access.note: The U.S. Lighthouse Society Digital Archive lists the light as not open to the public. Ownership and present access are not recorded in the sources read.

events.note: Small lighted beacon on a granite pier; fixed red light from a sixth-order Fresnel lens, from 4 November 1872 (D'Entremont).
Original lens: sixth-order Fresnel, year installed 1872 (Archive).
Further $15,000 appropriated 23 June 1874 for a combined lighthouse and dwelling (D'Entremont).
Wooden house and square tower on the enlarged granite pier; Archive gives tower established 1876; D'Entremont says finished early spring 1876.
Brutally cold winter; a steamer bound for New York City became lodged in the ice (D'Entremont).
Keeper William Tengren rescued two men and two women from drowning after their boat overturned about half a mile from the station (30 June).
Keeper William Tengren rescued a man exhausted while trying to swim from Gaspee Point to the lighthouse (16 August).
Keeper Andrew Zuius rescued two persons from a sailboat that capsized in a squall (27 May).
September 1938 hurricane: dwelling not habitable and tower unsafe (Lighthouse Service Bulletin); Archive disposition 'Damaged in 1938 Hurricane'.
Archive gives year discontinued as 1938; D'Entremont says discontinued shortly after the storm.

corrections.why: The wooden 1876 house-and-tower was damaged in the September 1938 hurricane and was later torn down (D'Entremont; Archive disposition 'Damaged in 1938 Hurricane'). The structure on the old foundation today is a skeleton tower, not the 1876 wooden tower the record lists as standing.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Archive and D'Entremont both date the first light and its sixth-order lens to 1872: a small beacon on a granite pier. The 1876 date is the house and tower built on the enlarged pier, so the 1872 start is kept and 1876 is noted as the tower's date.
The Archive gives 48 feet above mean high water (14.6 m), which the facts use. The record's 8.8 m and Wikidata's 9.0 m are not explained by any source read.
The sources read describe the 1872 light as fixed red from a sixth-order lens (D'Entremont). The record's 'Oc W 4s' is not dated by any source read and is not used for the 1872 to 1938 light.
The Archive gives 1938 as the year discontinued, and D'Entremont says discontinued shortly after the storm. A 1939 date in the record (Wikidata) is not supported by the sources read.
The 1876 wooden tower is not standing; see corrections. The standing structure on the foundation is a later skeleton tower.

notes_for_editor: 1) The 1872 first lighting, the $1,000 (1872) and $15,000 (1874) appropriations, the 4 November 1872 date, the 1876 finish and the 1907 fog bell rest on D'Entremont alone; the Lighthouse Board volumes for 1872 to 1890 are not in the local corpus, and newspaper searches for November 1872 found nothing usable. Check against the Lighthouse Board reports for fiscal 1873 to 1876 when they are added. 2) Wikipedia (leads only, not cited) gives a different 1872 story: a portable beacon kept by the Sabin Point keepers, lit in 1876. Left out until a primary source confirms it. Wikipedia also has Tengren 1918-1927, Zuius 1927-1939 and a 1939 transfer of Zuius to Palmer Island; none is cited here. 3) The Archive's roster gives Tengren at Bullock's Point from 1916; D'Entremont and the 1918 Commissioner list say 1918. Both are recorded; the story says the Archive's date and D'Entremont's. 4) Zuius: the Archive says Sr. (1926-1939); D'Entremont says 1927-1938. The Bulletins' 1925 to 1927 'Andrew Zuius, jr.' at Old Orchard Shoal (New York) is a different keeper and is not linked to this station. 5) The $3,600 riprap figure (fiscal 1918 estimates) comes from an OCR table. The row reads 'Bullocks Point, R. 1 3,600', with the name and figure on one line. The 2026-10-28 fact-check read the archive.org page image (scan page 378, printed page 64) in the viewer, and the Bullocks Point row carries the figure at the resolution the viewer gave. 6) The 1913 Mussel Bed Shoal line is OCR'd as 'Mussel Bed Shoa,]'; matched by context. The Mussel Bed Shoal stint (1909 to 1916, Archive) is not cited from the Mussel Bed record here; only the 1913 Bulletin is cited for it. 7) Printed page numbers for the Lighthouse Board and Commissioner volumes are not confirmed from the page images; scan page numbers are given. Bulletin citations use PDF pages. 8) The USCG Historian's page for Bullock's Point (history.uscg.mil) could not be read through the Internet Archive (403 and 404), so no USCG history is used. 9) The 1938 Bulletin calls the river the North Providence River; the Archive gives Providence River Channel. Not resolved; the story says Providence River. 10) Present owner, access and whether the pier can be reached are not in any source read; the story says the Archive lists the light as not open to the public and advises against landing or climbing. 11) The 1938 Bulletin's account of the 1938 storm damage names the Bullock's Point dwelling and tower; the Prudence Island account on the same page is not used here.
